Fibrinogen Repletion
The minimum fibrinogen content per unit of 
cryoprecipitate is specified as 50 mg/unit but 
the actual concentration can vary considera-
bly (300–3000 mg dl–1). The “standard” cryo-
precipitate dose of 0.1–0.2 units kg–1 is 
expected to increase fibrinogen levels by 
75  mg dl–1 but doses of 0.5–1.0 units kg–1 
(5–10 ml kg–1) are commonly administered 
to neonates and infants following complex 
procedures. Fibrinogen concentrate can be 
used in place of cryoprecipitate at a dose of 
70 mg kg–1 or using the equation from the 
package insert: dose = (target level − measured 
level)/1.7 × weight (kg), to reach a target 
level. Generally, a target fibrinogen concen-
tration >150–200 mg dl–1 is sought. It should 
be kept in mind that cryoprecipitate is a non-
purified blood product and in addition to 
fibrinogen, it contains fibronectin and plate-
let microparticles, and coagulation factors 
VIII, XIII, and von Willebrand factor.
Prothrombin Complex Concentrates (PCC), 
rVIIA, Desmopressin Administration
The decision to administer rFVIIa or a PCC 
for hemostasis should be based on surgeon 
and anesthesiologist assessment that refrac-
tory bleeding despite maximal, standard 
blood component therapy is present and the 
recognition that these agents are strongly pro-
thrombotic. Particular caution should be used 
when administering these agents to patients 
with structures at risk for thrombosis such as 
mBTTT shunts or small ascending aortas.
Prothrombin complex concentrates are for-
mulations containing vitamin K-­dependent 
clotting factors. PCCs are classified as four-­
factor prothrombin complex concentrates 
(4FPCCs) containing factors II, VII, IX, and X, 
and three-­factor prothrombin complex

Antifibrinolytics
Because activation of the fibrinolytic path-
way plays an important role in the coagulop-
athy observed during and after cardiac 
surgery, prophylactic administration of anti-
fibrinolytic agents in neonates and children 
undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB is 
­relatively routine. Currently available antifi-
brinolytic agents are the lysine analogs 
tranexamic 
acid 
(TXA) 
and 
epsilon-­
aminocaproic acid (Amicar®) which competi-
tively inhibit the binding of TPA and 
plasminogen to the lysine residues on fibrin. 
This inhibits formation of plasmin and thus 
degradation of fibrin. Plasmin generation 
after tissue injury also induces thrombin 
generation, complement activation, and acti-
vation of monocytes, neutrophils, and plate-
lets. Thus there are potential advantanges 
to higher plasma levels of these agents. 
Unfortunately, there is no consensus on the 
optimal plasma levels of these agents and 
hence there is great institutional variation in 
dosing regimens. There is also concern that 
high plasma levels of both TXA and Amicar 
are associated with seizures as a result of 
enhanced neuronal excitation due to their 
interactions with gamma-­aminobutyric acid 
(GABA) and glycine receptor-­mediated neu-
rotransmission. A summary of the dosing 
schedules to obtain target plasma levels of 
TXA and Amicar across various age groups 
is given in Table 7.6.

Echocardiography is an indispensable tool in 
the diagnosis and management of congenital 
heart disease.
Transthoracic 
Echocardiography
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is 
the primary imaging tool in the diagnosis 
and assessment of congenital and acquired 
heart disease in neonates, infants, children, 
and adolescents. A complete TTE exam is 
noninvasive, can be performed on site any-
where, and provides detailed anatomic, 
hemodynamic, and physiologic information. 
It is particularly valuable in neonates, infants, 
and children, given their smaller size, as a 
shallower depth of penetration of the ultra-
sound beam is needed to image the heart, 
compared to adults.
Image resolution and depth of penetration 
are inversely related, with higher frequency 
transducers having higher resolution but less 
depth of penetration. High-­frequency probes 
(8 or 12  MHz) focus at depths of 4–5  cm, 
whereas low-­ or mid-­frequency probes (2.5, 
3, 5  MHz) focus at depths of 12–16  cm. 
Consequently, a high-­frequency transducer 
with excellent image resolution can be used 
in infants and neonates, whereas the depth of 
penetration necessary to image an adolescent 
or adult will necessitate use of a lower fre-
quency probe with poorer image resolution.
The imaging widows typically used in a 
comprehensive TTE exam are shown in 
Figure  8.1. Figures  8.2–8.9 summarize the 
images obtained during a comprehensive 
TTE exam.
Transesophageal 
Echocardiography
Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is 
a valuable, semiinvasive imaging modality 
which allows monitoring and diagnostic 
imaging of the heart before, during, and after 
cardiac or noncardiac procedures without 
interruption. The esophageal position of the 
ultrasonic transducer provides imaging with-
out the constraints imposed by the interposi-
tion of the chest wall and lungs between the 
TTE transducer and the heart. In addition, 
TEE provides better visualization of poste-
rior cardiac structures such as the left and 
right atrium and the pulmonary veins given 
its direct proximity to these structures. 
Figures 8.10 and 8.11 summarize terminol-
ogy used to describe manipulation of the 
TEE probe, the four standard transducer 
positions within the esophagus and stomach, 
and the conventions of image display. It 
should be noted that in some pediatric insti-
tutions, the vertex of the displayed image is 
inverted (vertex at the bottom of the screen 
rather than the top) compared to what is 
shown in Figure 8.11. Figures 8.12–8.17 sum-
marize the images obtained during a com-
prehensive TEE exam.

for intraoperative use in neonates, infants,

and children. Two-­dimensional TEE probes

and 3D TEE probes are available for use in

These probes possess two-­dimensional,

and M-­mode capabilities. Although intraop-

­ventilation, inadvertent tracheal extubation, 
right main stem bronchial intubation, 
esophageal perforation, aortic arch com-
pression with loss of distal perfusion, and 
compression of the left atrium resulting in 
left atrial hypertension or compromise of 
ventricular filling. In particular, ante-­ or 
­retroflexion of the probe must be performed 
with caution in small patients.
Absolute contraindications to placement 
of a TEE probe in a child under anesthesia 
are:
●
●unrepaired tracheoesophageal fistula
●
●esophageal obstruction or stricture
●
●perforated hollow viscus
●
●active gastric or esophageal bleeding.
Relative contraindications to placement of a

●
●history of esophageal or gastric surgery
●
●history of esophageal cancer
●
●esophageal varices or diverticulum
●
●recent gastrointestinal bleed
●
●active esophagitis or peptic ulcer disease
●
●vascular ring or aortic arch anomaly 
wherein placement of the probe is likely to 
cause airway or vascular compromise
●
●oropharyngeal pathology
●
●severe coagulopathy including significant 
thrombocytopenia
●
●cervical spine injury or anomaly
●

The role of TEE in the detection of resid-
ual ventricular septal defects (VSDs) fol-
lowing the repair of both simple and 
complex defects deserves some discussion. 
Residual defects <3  mm are detectable by 
TEE but generally do not require immedi-
ate reoperation as they are hemodynami-
cally insignificant. The majority (75%) of 
these small defects are not present at the 
time of hospital discharge, as determined 
by TTE. Residual defects of 3–4  mm 
detected by TEE require further analysis 
with intraoperative oximetry to determine 
the ratio of pulmonary to systemic blood 
flow (QP:QS) and hemodynamic data to 
measure left atrial pressure (LAP) and pul-
monary artery pressure (PAP). A residual 
defect ≥4 mm or a lesion associated with a 
QP:QS >1.5:1 likely requires a return to CPB 
for an additional attempt at closure.

Epicardial Echocardiography
Transesophageal echocardiography imaging 
of some cardiac structures, such as the distal 
ascending aorta, aortic arch, right ventricular 
outflow tract, and pulmonary artery bifurca-
tion, may be suboptimal due to the interposi-
tion of the trachea and main bronchi between 
the transducer and structures of interest. In 
addition, it may be difficult to align the 
Doppler beam parallel to some cardiac struc-
tures, resulting in Doppler spectra that will 
underestimate the true velocity and thus the 
calculated gradient. Surgeon-­performed epi-
cardial imaging can be used as an adjuvant to 
TEE imaging to overcome these limitations. It 
provides an unlimited number of imaging

Thus, a normal heart would have (S,D,S)

would give (S,D,D) segmental anatomy. 
Whereas most people with normal segmen-

with congenital heart disease (HLHS, TOF,

Atrial Identity and Location
The identity of the atrial chamber can best be 
determined by examining appendage anat-
omy. The right atrial appendage (RAA) is 
best seen in the transverse plane. Flexion of 
the probe will allow better visualization. The 
RAA has the following characteristics:
●
●a broad junction with the right atrium 
(RA)
●
●it is short and blunt (Snoopy’s nose).
The left atrial appendage is seen in multiple 
views. It has the following characteristics:
●
●a narrow junction with the LA
●
●it is long, narrow, and crenulated (Snoopy’s 
ear).
The SVC and IVC normally return to the RA, 
as does the coronary sinus when it is not 
unroofed into the posterior wall of the LA. The 
pulmonary veins normally return to the LA. 
The RA will have a Eustachian valve; the LA 
septal surface has the flap of the fossa ovalis.
In patients with heterotaxy syndrome, 
both atria have systemic and pulmonary 
venous connections and the atria themselves 
may have ambiguous morphology. The entry 
points of the SVC and pulmonary veins into 
the atrial chambers can exhibit considerable 
variability in heterotaxy syndrome. In some 
of these patients, the IVC is interrupted 
between the kidneys and liver and the hepatic 
veins drain directly either to the floor of the 
right-­sided atrium (situs solitus) or the left-­
sided atrium (situs invertus). The infrahe-
patic portion of the IVC drains via the 
azygous or hemiazygous system to a right-­ or 
left-­sided SVC.
Ventricular Size and Identity
A chamber is considered a ventricle if it 
receives more than 50% of the ventricular inlet 
(fibrous ring of an AV valve). The AV valve 
need not be patent for the chamber to be con-
sidered a ventricle, as is the case with tricuspid 
or mitral atresia. Likewise, the chamber does 
not need to be large to be considered a ventri-
cle, as is the case with hypoplastic left heart 
syndrome. In the absence of any AV connec-
tion (as in double inlet LV), the chamber is 
called a bulboventricular foramen (BVF).
The right and left ventricles have different 
morphologies.
●
●Right ventricle:
–
– has the tricuspid valve (three leaflets) 
with a chordal attachment to the sep-
tum via one of the leaflets; there are 
three papillary muscles that are located 
apically
–
– the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve 
inserts slightly lower on the intraven-
tricular septum than the anterior leaflet 
of the mitral valve, creating the ventric-
uloatrial septum (VAS) which separates 
the RA from the LV. A defect in this area 
is the source of a Gerbode defect (LV to 
RA shunt)
–
– has a triangular shape and a trabecu-
lated endocardial surface
–
– has the moderator band, a band of tissue 
that stretches from the lower intraven-
tricular septum to the anterior RV wall 
and is best seen in the four-­chamber 
view with retroflexion of the TEE probe
–
– there is conus or an infundibulum in the 
RV; this creates a lack of fibrous conti-
nuity between the tricuspid valve and 
pulmonary valve.
●
●Left ventricle:
–
– has the mitral valve (two leaflets) with 
no chordal attachment to the septum; 
there are two papillary muscles that are 
located at the junction of the apical and 
middle two-­thirds of the chamber
Echocardiography
99
–
– has an ellipsoid shape and a smooth 
endocardial surface
–
– there is no conus or infundibulum in the 
LV; as a result, there is fibrous continu-
ity between the mitral valve and aortic 
valve.
Atrioventricular Relationship
Normally there is atrioventricular con-
cordance (RA to RV, LA to LV) due to the 
presence of situs solitus and D loop ventri-
cles; atrioventricular concordance can also 
exist in the presence of situs invertus and 
L  loop ventricles. Atrioventricular dis-
cordance (RA to LV, LA to RV) exists in 
the presence of situs solitus and L loop 
­ventricles or situs invertus and D loop 
­ventricles. It is important to remember 
that the morphology of the AV valve in 
both atrioventricular concordance and 
atrioventricular discordance is determined 
by the morphology of the corresponding 
ventricle, not the atria.
Great Vessel Orientation and Identity
Normally, the great vessels are oriented at 
45° to each other when they leave the heart, 
with the pulmonary artery (PA) anterior to 
the aorta. When they are viewed echocardio-
graphically, one vessel will be observed in the 
short axis and the other will have a sausage 
shape. When the great vessels are trans-
posed, they are oriented parallel to each 
other when they leave the heart. When they 
are viewed echocardiographically, both ves-
sels will be observed in the same axis. The 
rule of thumb when viewing transposed ves-
sels in the short axis is that the anterior vessel 
is invariably the aorta. When the vessels are 
aligned side by side, the determination is 
more difficult and usually requires finding 
the arch of the aorta, the coronary arteries, 
or the branch pulmonary arteries to make 
the determination.
After the great vessels are identified, 
their relationship to the ventricles must 
be delineated. This requires creativity in 
­finding the views that allow this connec-
tion to be seen.
Ventriculoarterial Relationship
Normally there is ventriculoarterial con-
cordance (RV to PA, LV to Ao); ventricu-
loarterial discordance (LV to PA, RV to Ao) 
is transposition. If the aorta is anterior and 
rightward of the PA, it is dextro (D); if the 
aorta is anterior and leftward of the PA, it is 
levo (L). As a rule, it is the relationship of 
the great arteries to each other (side by 
side, anterior/posterior) and to the ventri-
cles that determines the relationship of the 
great vessels to a VSD rather than the posi-
tion of the VSD itself. For example, in dou-
ble outlet RV (DORV), what determines 
whether a VSD is subpulmonary or subaor-
tic is both the position of the VSD (it is usu-
ally conoventricular) and the position of 
the great vessels relative to the VSD. 
Another key feature in DORV is the pres-
ence of bilateral conus; neither the tricus-
pid valve nor the mitral valve is in fibrous 
continuity with the pulmonary valve or the 
aortic valve.
In tetralogy of Fallot there is aortic over-­
ride over the RV but the mitral valve is in 
fibrous continuity with the aortic valve (NOT 
DORV). In d-­transposition of the great arter-
ies (D-­TGA), there is fibrous continuity 
between the mitral valve and pulmonary 
valve and conus between the tricuspid valve 
and aortic valve (NOT DORV).
Presence of Intracardiac Shunts 
and Obstructive Lesions
Color flow (CF) Doppler is indispensable in 
identifying intracardiac shunts, including 
those not seen with two-­dimensional imag-
ing. Continuous-­wave (CW) Doppler is use-
ful in determining velocities and gradients 
across restrictive communications or valves, 
whereas pulsed-­wave (PW) Doppler can be 
used to assess less restrictive orifices as well 
as hepatic and pulmonary venous blood flow. 
The RVOT must be examined carefully for 
The Pediatric Cardiac Anesthesia Handbook
100
both dynamic and fixed obstructive lesions. 
Two-­dimensional echocardiography in com-
bination with Doppler will clearly delineate 
dynamic obstructive lesions. The use of CW 
Doppler to determine intracardiac pressures 
is also valuable. Do not forget to look for a 
PDA.
Evaluation of the Surgical Repair
A comprehensive preoperative TEE study is 
the foundation of repair assessment. This 
allows the operator to focus the examination 
on the repaired lesions. Look for the com-
mon things, detailed below.
Patch Leaks
After ventricular septal defect (VSD) and atrial 
septal defect (ASD) repairs, detection of resid-
ual VSD leaks can be more difficult than it 
sounds, because the VSD patch produces areas 
of echo attenuation in the RV and RVOT that 
may mask leaks. Multiplane imaging improves 
detection but does not completely resolve this 
problem. It may be difficult to distinguish CFD 
flow from a perimembranous VSD from a TR 
jet. CW Doppler, however, can be useful in this 
scenario. For example, assuming:
Systolic blood pressure = 120 mmHg
RVSP = 39 mmHg
CVP =14 mmHg
If the peak velocity by CW Doppler is 
4.5 m/sec, then the gradient is 81 mmHg and 
the defect is a VSD. If the peak velocity is 
2.5 m/sec, then the gradient is 25 mmHg and 
the defect is TR.
Baffle Obstruction
●
●Fontan baffle evaluation requires careful 
examination with CF Doppler, looking for 
subtle evidence of flow acceleration in 
what is a low-­velocity venous pathway. In 
addition, the baffle fenestration, if present, 
must be evaluated for patency, pressure 
gradient, and direction of flow.
●
●Senning, Mustard (baffling of systemic and 
pulmonary venous blood).
Stenotic Valves
After valvuloplasty regarding mitral stenosis, 
the following grades are generally used.
●
●Insignificant = pulsed/CW Doppler mean 
gradient ≤5 mmHg.
●
●Potentially 
significant 
= 
pulsed/CW 
Doppler mean gradient of 5–8 mmHg.
●
●Significant = pulsed/CW Doppler mean 
gradient of >8 mmHg. A mean mitral valve 
inflow gradient of more than 5–7 mmHg 
has been suggested as a cut-­off point for 
consideration of further repair or valve 
replacement.
Regurgitant Valves
●
●After valvuloplasty but also after transval-
vular approaches to lesions (such as trans-­
tricuspid or pulmonary valve approach to a 
VSD).
●
●Regarding mitral regurgitation, the follow-
ing classifications are generally used in 
conjunction with objective data such as the 
width of the vena contracta.
–
– Insignificant = absent or trivial regurgi-
tation jet width (<2  mm) by color 
Doppler at the level of the valve leaflets.
–
– Potentially significant = regurgitant jet 
width 2–4 mm by color Doppler at the 
level of the valve leaflets.
–
– Significant = regurgitant jet width 
>4 mm by color Doppler at the level of 
the valve leaflets. Return to bypass for 
further correction or valve replacement 
is often considered for more than mild 
MR, due to the increased risk for 
reoperation.
Stenotic Anastomoses
●
●Pulmonary vein anastomosis to LA in total 
or partially anomalous pulmonary venous 
return.
●
●SVC to PA in bidirectional cavopulmonary 
connection and Fontan.
●
●Residual outflow tract gradients:
–
– after tetralogy of Fallot repairs
–
– after resection of subaortic membranes 
or LVOT reconstruction.
Echocardiography
101
●
●Residual gradients across fenestrated atrial 
or ventricular septum (TOF repair).
●
●Residual gradients across ASD or VSD left 
open in the course of a staged repair (tri-
cuspid atresia, TOF with pulmonary atre-
sia, hypoplastic left heart syndrome).
●
●Coronary artery imaging and patency: 
must be evaluated following any procedure 
involving coronary artery reimplantation 
or translocation:
–
– arterial switch for transposition of the

–
– aortic translocation such as Nikaidoh 
procedure
–
– Ross procedure (transplantation of the 
pulmonic valve to the aortic valve position 
and creation of an RV-­to-­PA conduit)
–
– anomalous aortic origin of a coronary

–
– anomalous origin of the left or right cor-

(ALCAPA and ARCAPA).
Ventricular Function Assessment
●
●After all repairs.
●
●Particular attention should be paid to (1) 
patients with reimplanted or translocated 
coronary arteries and (2) patients who may 
have had air in the coronary arteries dur-
ing the de-­airing process.
Patency of Aortopulmonary Shunts
Continuous-­wave Doppler will detect a high-­
velocity signal with flow in systole and 
­diastole. CF Doppler will help position the 
CW Doppler beam.
Patency of Cavopulmonary Shunts
Pulsed-­wave Doppler will reveal a phasic 
venous blood flow pattern that exhibits res-
piratory variation.

Risk scores have been developed to predict 
perioperative morbidity and mortality in 
children with CHD undergoing cardiac surgery 
or diagnostic and interventional cardiac 
catheterization procedures. Scores have also 
been developed to delineate risk for patients 
with CHD undergoing noncardiac procedures. 
Development of a risk assessment tool requires 
rigorous statistical analysis to derive the 
components of the score from a representative 
derivation cohort, followed by validation of the 
score in a separate validation cohort.
Cardiac Surgery
The Society of Thoracic Surgeons European 
Association for Thoracic Surgery (STAT) 
mortality category groups operative proce-
dures 
into 
five 
risk 
categories, 
with 
group 1 having the lowest mortality risk and 
5  having the highest (www.sts.org/sites/
default/files/CHSD%20Appendix%20C%20 
-­%20STAT%20Categories.pdf).
The 
Society 
of 
Thoracic 
Surgeons 
Congenital Heart Surgery Database provides 
risk-­adjusted mortality rates defined by 
patient age and primary procedure. Other 
risk scores include Risk Adjustment for 
Congenital Heart Surgery (RACHS) which 
groups operative procedures into six catego-
ries based on mortality (Table 9.1).
Catheterization
The Congenital Cardiac Catheterization 
Project on Outcomes (C3PO) includes four 
procedure-­type risk categories with cases 
classified based on the expected risk of 
­clinically important adverse events (AEs). 
However, C3PO is not structured to account 
for advancements in technology and new 
interventions.
Other procedure risk category methodolo-
gies have also been developed by the 
Congenital Cardiac Interventional Study 
Consortium (CCISC) and the Improving 
Pediatric and Adult Congenital Treatment 
(IMPACT) registries. The CCISC model, 
Catheterization Risk Score for Pediatrics 
(CRISP), which was developed in 2015, uses 
only three categories of procedure risk 
(Table 9.2). Similar to C3PO, it is not struc-
tured to assess the risk of new interventions. 
In addition, the hemodynamic risk compo-
nent used in C3PO, CRISP, and IMPACT 
assigns equal significance to all abnormal 
hemodynamic variables.
More 
recently, 
the 
Procedural 
Risk 
in 
Congenital 
Cardiac 
Catheterization 
(PREDIC3T) score was created (Table  9.3). 
Multivariate analysis of the PREDIC3T score, 
the hemodynamic vulnerability score, and 
age has been conducted to provide odds 
ratios for the occurrence of high-­severity

Noncardiac Procedures
Using the large ACS NSQIP database (www. 
facs.org/quality-­programs/data-­and-­ 
registries/acs-­nsqip/) 
and 
the 
NSQIP 
­definitions of mild, moderate, and severe 
CHD based on residual lesion burden and 
functional capacity, a rigorously derived risk 
assessment model for in-­hospital mortality 
following noncardiac surgical procedures in 
children with major and severe CHD was 
developed. A derivation cohort of 4375 (ACS 
NSQIP years 2012–2013) and a validation 
cohort of 2869 (ACS NSQIP year 2014) 
patients were used. Multivariable analysis 
was utilized to predict mortality and eight 
preoperative predictors were retained in a 
final multivariable logistic regression model 
as summarized in Table 9.5.
These variables were used to create a risk 
stratification score ranging from 0 to 10 
that showed very good calibration and 
discrimination in the validation cohort (area 
under the curve: 0.831 [95% CI 0.787–0.875]). 
Scores ≤3  were associated with low risk of 
mortality (OR 1.54, 95% CI 0.78–3.04), scores 
ranging from 4 to 6  were associated with 
medium risk (OR 4.19, 95% CI 2.56–6.87), 
and scores ≥7 were associated with high risk 
(OR 22.15, 95% CI 15.06–32.59). The 
influence of surgical complexity, as defined by 
both RVUs and surgical specialty on outcome, 
were not sufficiently strong to be retained 
in the final model. Both survivors and 
nonsurvivors underwent surgery of similar 
complexity as defined by RVUs. This suggests 
that the presence of major and severe CHD is

Extracorporeal Membrane 
Oxygenation
Extracorporeal 
membrane 
oxygenation 
(ECMO), also known as extracorporeal life 
support (ECLS), is a technology used to pro-
vide cardiopulmonary (venoarterial ECMO) 
or pulmonary (venovenous ECMO) support 
for patients with cardiac, pulmonary, and 
cardiopulmonary failure that is unresponsive 
to medical therapies.
Indications
In pediatric practice, ECMO is used to provide 
support in a wide variety of circumstances, 
including respiratory failure, circulatory fail-
ure (viral myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, post 
cardiac surgery [postcardiotomy support]), 
persistent pulmonary hypertension of the 
newborn, meconium aspiration syndrome, 
respiratory distress syndrome, group B 
­streptococcal sepsis, asphyxia, congenital 
diaphragmatic hernia, and sepsis. ECMO is 
also used to assist cardiopulmonary resusci-
tation (E-­CPR), and as a bridge to organ 
transplantation and ventricular assist device 
placement.
Relative Contraindications
Relative contraindications to ECMO include 
end-­stage primary disease, severe neurologic 
injury, intracranial bleeding, prematurity 
(<34th week), uncontrolled visceral bleeding, 
low birth weight (<2 kg), and patient or fam-
ily wishes.
Modes of ECMO Support
A typical ECMO circuit consists of a mechan-
ical pump (centrifugal or roller), a membrane 
oxygenator, venous and arterial cannulas, a 
reservoir, heat exchanger, tubing, and pres-
sure, flow and oxygen saturation monitors 
(Figure 10.1).
Two distinct modes of ECMO are availa-
ble, namely venoarterial (VA) and veno-
venous (VV).
Venovenous (VV) ECMO
●
●Access is generally percutaneous via the 
internal jugular vein.
●
●Used for prolonged pulmonary support in 
patients with respiratory failure with 
­preserved cardiac function.
10
Mechanical Circulatory Support
The Pediatric Cardiac Anesthesia Handbook
110
●
●Blood is drained from the venous circulation 
and returned to the venous circulation 
after exchange of oxygen and carbon 
­dioxide in the membrane.
Venoarterial (VA) ECMO
●
●Access can be percutaneous via the inter-
nal jugular vein and the carotid artery, but 
generally direct surgical exposure of the 
vessels is required. In the postcardiotomy 
setting access is commonly obtained 
directly via the right atrium and aorta.
●
●Used for prolonged cardiac and pulmonary 
support.
●
●Blood is drained from the venous circulation 
and pumped into the arterial circulation 
after heat exchange and exchange of 
­oxygen and carbon dioxide.
●
●Cardiac output is a combination of the 
native cardiac ejection and ECMO flow. 
Consequently, an appropriate quantity of 
alveolar ventilation is necessary when 
venous blood transits the pulmonary 
­circulation. When all venous drainage is 
captured, VA-­ECMO closely resembles 
total CPB. When only a portion of venous 
return is captured, VA-­ECMO resembles 
partial CPB.
The operational differences between VA-­
ECMO and VV-­ECMO are summarized in 
Table 10.1, while functional differences in the 
physiologic parameters monitored are sum-
marized in Table 10.2.

Intraoperative Considerations for Patients 
on ECMO
1)  Particular attention during transport to 
and from the operating room is a must to 
avoid decannulation and kinking of the 
cannula.
2)  Expect significant blood loss due to 
­heparinization, thrombocytopenia, and 
coagulation factor deficits (ensure ade-
quate vascular access and blood product 
availability).
3)  Volatile agents have altered kinetics in 
patients on ECMO, and reduced alveolar 
ventilation may reduce volatile anesthetic 
delivery.
4)  Hemodynamics of patients on VV-­ECMO 
are dependent on their native heart func-
tion; it may become necessary to support 
the circulation with vasopressors and/or 
inotropes.
5)  Patients on VA-­ECMO are often receiv-
ing vasopressor/inotrope therapy before 
ECMO institution, and are likely to 
require 
vasopressor/inotrope 
therapy 
during the ECMO run.
6)  During VA-­ECMO ventricular ejection of 
blood, as indicated by a pulsatile arterial 
waveform, will occur whenever there is 
return of venous blood to the systemic 
ventricle AND when there is sufficient 
ventricular contractile function to open 
the aortic valve. Return of venous blood 
to the systemic ventricle in the absence of 
sufficient ventricular contractile function 
to open the aortic valve will result in ven-
tricular distention.
7)  During VV-­ECMO and VA-­ECMO runs, 
the lungs should be ventilated at low

Ventricular Assist Devices
In 1967, DeBakey and colleagues used a left-­
atrial–axillary artery ventricular assist device 
(VAD) to provide postcardiotomy ventricu-
lar support to a 16-­year-­old girl. This was the 
earliest report of VAD use in a pediatric 
patient. Since then, major advances in tech-
nology have occurred, accompanied by 
improved outcomes. During the past decade, 
as device technology has matured, devices 
specifically designed for smaller pediatric 
patients have been developed for clinical use.
Indications
In pediatric practice, the size of the child, the 
indication for support, and the presumed 
duration of support are the important con-
siderations when choosing a VAD.
VAD use can be summarized as follows.
●
●A bridge to recovery: in this setting, devices 
suitable for short-­term support are utilized 
with the intent to wean the patient off 
device support and remove the device after 
recovery of cardiopulmonary function. 
Myocarditis and postcardiotomy patients 
are suitable candidates for this type of 
support.
●
●A bridge to decision: in this setting, devices 
suitable for short-­term support are utilized 
with the intent of determining over time 
whether patients with suspected severe 
end-­organ dysfunction (particularly neu-
rologic) are suitable candidates for 
recovery, longer term support, or cardiac 
transplantation.
●
●A bridge to transplantation: in this set-
ting, devices suitable for long-­term sup-
port are utilized with the intent of 
providing cardiopulmonary support until 
cardiac transplantation. Converting from 
a short-­term device to a long-­term device 
to await transplantation is known as 
“bridge-­to-­bridge.”
●
●Destination therapy: in this setting, 
devices suitable for long-­term support are 
utilized with the intent of providing per-
manent support for patients who are not 
deemed suitable candidates for cardiac 
transplantation.
Relative Contraindications
In complex situations such as concomitant 
respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension 
and residual intracardiac shunts, VAD 
­support may be contraindicated.
Current VAD and TAH Technologies
Current VAD and TAH technologies include 
pneumatic pulsatile flow and continuous non-
pulsatile (axial or centrifugal) flow devices.
Pneumatic Pulsatile Flow Devices

Pulsatile Pump Technology
A rigid case prosthetic ventricle is divided 
into a blood and a pneumatic chamber 
by  a  flexible, noncompliant diaphragm. 
Unidirectional inflow and outflow valves are 
located in the blood chamber. The pneu-
matic chamber communicates with the 
pneumatic drive system via the pneumatic 
driveline. As pressurized air is introduced 
into the pneumatic chamber, the diaphragm 
moves such that the blood chamber becomes 
pressurized as well. When the pressure in the 
blood chamber exceeds the device filling 
pressure, the inflow valve will close. When 
pressure in the blood chamber exceeds aortic 
or pulmonary artery pressure, the outflow 
valve opens and ejection commences. These 
processes constitute the isovolemic and 
ejection phases of systole in the prosthetic 
ventricle. Depending on the device, the 
driveline pressures are set approximately 
80–100 mmHg higher than systemic systolic 
pressure for LVAD and 30–80 mmHg higher 
than pulmonary artey pressure for RVAD.
At the end of systole, air is vented passively 
from the pneumatic chamber to the atomo-
sphere and the pressure in the blood chamber 
falls. This constitutes isovolemic relaxation.

prosthetic ventricle (right atrium, left atrium, 
or left ventricle) exceeds the pressure in the 
blood chamber, the inflow valve opens. The 
diaphragm is free to move in such a manner 
that virtually the entire volume of the pros-
thetic ventricle can fill with blood as all the 
air leaves the pneumatic chamber. This con-
stitutes diastole in the prosthetic ventricle. 
Vacuum pressure of -­20 to -­40 mmHg. can be 
applied to the pneumatic chamber during 
diastole to promote filling.
The Berlin VAD always and the SynCardia 
TAH generally function in a fixed rate, vari-
able stroke volume mode. In general, pump 
rates are kept low (60–80 bpm) with the per-
centage of systole set to equal one-­half the 
device rate (percentage of systole at 60 bpm = 
30%; percentage of systole at 80 bpm = 40%). 
These settings promote complete filling and 
emptying of the device, which is important 
because these devices function in fixed rate, 
variable stroke volume capacity. Increases in 
applied vacuum, higher driveline pressures, 
and reduced percent systole all increase the 
likelihood that blood trauma and hemolysis 
will occur.
The Thoratec PVAD can function in both 
the fixed rate, variable stroke volume mode 
and a fixed stroke volume, variable rate 
mode. This fill-­to-­empty mode is feasible 
because the movement of the pump dia-
phragm is monitored by a Hall sensor built 
into the rigid case. A small magnet mounted 
on the diaphragm triggers the Hall sensor 
when the two come in contact. This informa-
tion is transmitted to the console via an elec-
trical cable and allows the control console to 
know when the blood chamber is full, trig-
gering ejection.

Axial Pump Technology
These compact pumps employ an impeller 
mechanism as the only moving part. At the 
proximal end of the pump, stationary airfoil-­
shaped vanes are used to straighten blood 
flow prior to entry into an impeller. The 
impeller then imparts radial velocity (kinetic 
energy) to the blood as it draws blood into 
the pump. At the distal end of the pump, a set 
of stationary diffuser (stator) vanes can be 
used to increase axial velocity by straighten-
ing flow. This improves conversion of kinetic 
energy to static pressure (potential energy) as 
blood leaves the pump. Axial pump rotating 
elements operate like a propeller in a pipe 
and can be viewed as a pusher. These pumps 
are small; the Impella crosses the aortic or 
pulmonary valve without inducing insuffi-
ciency and the HeartMate II is about the size 
of a D cell battery (Figure 10.5).

Pump output is determined by rpm and 
delta P (aortic pressure – LV pressure), also 
called the pressure head (H) (Figure  10.6). 
Axial flow pumps have steep pressure flow 
curves and as such, flow is inversely propor-
tional to delta P. For a given arterial pressure 
during nonpulsatile flow, a higher pump dif-
ferential pressure can only be generated by 
lowering ventricular pressure relative to aor-
tic pressure. The increasing pressure differen-
tial generated as flow decreases results in 
much higher suction developed at the inlet 
during conditions of low LV volume or inlet 
cannula obstruction.This means axial pumps 
pull the hardest at the lowest flow, creating 
the potential for a self-­latching condition 
wherein the pump continues to increase suc-
tion as flows fall, resulting in the ventricular 
wall being sucked in around the inlet. This 
results in suck-­down of the ventricular wall

Centrifugal Pump Technology
Centrifugal pumps use a constrained vortex 
to impart kinetic energy to fluid in a rotating 
head. The rotating head consists of a series 
of concentrically arranged cones or fins sus-
pended within a rigid plastic shell (volute).

Mechanical Circulatory Support
119
creates a contact-­free blood chamber due to 
the absence of bearings and seals, resulting 
in minimized blood stagnation, friction, and 
shear stress. Rotation of the cones or fins 
creates a vortex that is constrained by the 
rigid plastic housing. This creates lower 
pressure at the center of the pump than at 
the periphery. The pressure gradient draws 
blood into the center of the pump and 
imparts pressure to the blood as it leaves the 
pump at the periphery. In a centrifugal 
pump, its rotating elements act as a spinning 
disk with blades that can be viewed as a 
thrower.
As with axial flow pumps, centrifugal 
pump output is determined by rpm and 
inversely related to dP (aortic pressure – LV 
pressure). However, centrifugal flow pumps 
have flatter pressure–flow curves than axial 
pumps. A centrifugal flow pump responds 
only to the total differential pressure across 
the pump and not the absolute value of the 
pressures at the inlet and outlet ports. At any 
given pump speed, a centrifugal pump will 
have the same flow at inlet and outlet pres-
sure values respectively of 0/100, 100/200, 
and –50/50 mmHg, as the delta P is 100 mmHg. 
Because the flatter pressure–flow curve 
maintains a relatively fixed differential 
­pressure even with a large drop in pump flow, 
no significant increase in suction pressure 
is 
generated 
at 
low-­flow 
conditions 
(Figures 10.6 and 10.7).
Complications
The most common complications include 
bleeding, thrombosis, embolic events such as 
stroke, and infection.
Anesthetic Considerations for Patients 
Receiving VAD
End-­organ dysfunction in addition to cardiac 
dysfunction occurs in patients supported 
with VAD. In particular, renal and hepatic 
dysfunction should be evaluated.

Figure 10.7  Comparison of HQ curves (delta P versus flow) for a Heartmate 3 continuous centrifugal pump (A) 
and a HeartMate II continuous axial pump (B). Note that the centrifugal pump has a very flat portion of its HQ 
curve compared to the axial pump which is consistently steep. A pump with a flat HQ curve is more sensitive 
to afterload (small increases in delta P lead to large reductions in pump flow) than a pump with a steep HQ 
curve. On the other hand, a pump with a flat HQ curve is less prone to development of a suction event and 
pump shutdown than a pump with a steep curve. The HeartMate 3 is unique in that it has a flatter sloped HQ 
curve when operating at lower flows (<4 l min–1) and a steeper sloped HQ curve at higher flows (>4 l min–1).

The preoperative evaluation includes the 
following factors.
●
●Children with a glomerular filtration 
rate (GFR) <60 ml min–1 1.72 m2 should 
be assumed to have occult renal dys-
function and are at risk for acute renal 
injury or failure, even if blood urea 
nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine levels 
were normal.
●
●A full panel of liver function tests and a full 
coagulation profile should be performed to 
rule out hepatic dysfunction.
●
●Levels of B-­natriuretic peptide (BNP), a 
specific marker of elevated ventricular 
end-­diastolic pressure, are likely to be ele-
vated. Lethargy and anorexia in children 
strongly suggest the presence of a low car-
diac output state.
●
●Particular attention should be paid dur-
ing the physical examination to the 
assessment of arterial and venous access 
sites.
●
●A review of recent echocardiographic 
and cardiac catheterization data is 
essential.
●
●Pacemaker and/or implantable cardioverter 
defibrillators should be reprogrammed 
prior to surgery.
●
●The blood bank should be alerted to the 
possibility that a massive transfusion will 
be required. It is prudent to use leukocyte-­
reduced blood to minimize further antibody 
formation, as well as cytomegalovirus-­free 
blood products.
Induction of Anesthesia and Pre-­bypass 
Management
These patients have limited contractile 
reserve, limited preload recruitable stroke 
work, a limited ability to respond to acute 
increases or decreases in afterload, and a low 
cardiac output state. Thus, they require an 
induction that will blunt the hemodynamic 
response to laryngoscopy and tracheal 
­intubation 
without 
undue 
myocardial 
depression, vasodilation, and subsequent 
hypotension. 
Detailed 
management 
of 
patients with severely depressed ventricular 
function in covered in detail in Chapter 33 
but the following basic principles apply.
●
●Monitoring: 
American 
Society 
of 
Anesthesiologists 
monitoring, 
arterial, 
central venous pressure catheters and 
transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) 
probe should be utilized. Preoperative 
­inotropes should be continued.
●
●Mechanical 
ventilation: 
initiation 
of 
positive-­pressure ventilation is likely to 
induce significant pulse pressure variation, 
and needs to be initiated carefully with 
appropriate minute ventilation provided at 
the lowest possible mean airway pressure. 
Hypoventilation and atelectasis will increase 
pulmonary vascular resistance.
●
●Testing: serum lactate and mixed venous 
oxygen saturations are monitored as indi-
rect indicators of cardiac output. The use 
of the lysine analog antifibrinolytics 
tranexamic acid or epsilon-­aminocaproic 
acid should be considered.
Post-­VAD Placement Management
Continous-­flow devices have a preload sensi-
tivity (liters/min/mmHg) one-­third to one-­
quarter of that seen in the native LV and an 
afterload sensitivity 3–4 times that seen in 
the native LV. Centrifugal devices are slightly 
less preload sensitive and slightly more after-
load sensitive than axial devices. As the 
pump differential pressure changes between 
systole (smaller differential) and diastole 
(larger differential), pump flow is maximal 
during systole and lowest during diastole 
when LV pressure is lowest. Thus, pump flow 
during systole is assisted by intrinsic cardiac 
contraction, but flow in diastole reflects pre-
dominantly the work by the pump.
The flatter pressure–flow curves in cen-
trifugal pumps result in larger swings in flow 
from ventricular systole and diastole, pro-
ducing high pulsatility in pump flow in 
response to changing LV pressures during 
the cardiac cycle. Delta P is most effectively 
reduced by lowering aortic pressure (SVR 
reduction) or by increasing LV pressure 
(preload augmentation, LV contraction). In 
Mechanical Circulatory Support
121
fact, in the presence of increased LV contrac-
tility, semipulsatile flow may occur as the 
result of both aortic valve opening and cyclic 
increases in pump output with the dP reduc-
tion that accompanies LV contraction. These 
differences in the performance of axial versus 
centrifugal continuous flow pumps are sum-
marized in detail in Figures 10.6–10.8.

The Pediatric Cardiac Anesthesia Handbook

The pulsatility index (PI) is is a unitless 
measure calculated as beat-­to-­beat ampli-
tude between the maximal flows and mini-
mal flows averaged over 10–15 seconds and 
divided by the average flow according to the 
formula: 10 × [(maximum flow – minimum 
flow)/average flow]. From a practical per-
spective, pulsatility is a measure of the differ-
ence of pump flow between ventricular 
systole and diastole. Elevated blood pressure 
will increase the pressure differential across 
the pump and decrease flow, but the diastolic 
pressure gradient is affected more than the 
systolic gradient, and PI subsequently 
increases. The HeartMate 3 system utilizes 
the PI to recognize and avert a suction event. 
When the degree of pulsatility measured in 
the waveform falls below a preset value, the 
system regards this as a risk of a suction 
event and automatically lowers the rotor 
speed to a preset low speed limit and then 
gradually returns the rotor to its original 
speed.
The HeartMate 3 has an intrinsic pulsatil-
ity mechanism preprogrammed within the 
device, and is automatically active at a set 
rotor speed above 4000 rpm. The software is 
set to cycle every 2 seconds. Every 2 seconds, 
the rotor will decrease by 2000 rpm, from the 
set speed, for 0.15 seconds, then increase by 
4000 rpm for 0.20 seconds, and finally return 
to the set speed. This provides for 30 pulses/
min which promotes routine washing of the 
pump blood surfaces, which reduces the risk 
of blood stasis within the pump.
Right ventricle failure results in a decreased 
ability to fill the LV, thus decreasing the LV 
preload. Because the LVAD can only sense 
what is occurring in the LV, the decreased LV 
pressure seen in RV failure will resemble the 
pump parameters of hypovolemia, namely, 
decreased preload leads to a greater pressure 
gradient across the pump, thus decreasing 
flow and increasing the PI.
Left ventricular assist device insertion 
results in a global impairment of RV systolic 
function due to loss of the LV contribution to 
RV function. In addition, LVAD implantation 
generally acutely decreases mitral regurgita-
tion while worsening tricuspid regurgitation, 
both acutely and chronically. Poor apposition 
of the tricuspid valve leaflets after LV decom-
pression with a LVAD occurs as the result of 
a leftward shift of the intraventricular sep-
tum and the increased RV volume load. 
There is generally dilation of the tricuspid 
annulus and a leftward deviation of the septal 
components of the tricuspid subvalvular 
(chordae and papillary muscles) apparatus. 
Normally, this is offset by an increased right 
ventricular preload and a reduced right ven-
tricular afterload (due to a reduction in LA 
pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance 
[PVR]) such that right ventricular output is 
maintained or increased.
Treatment of right ventricular dysfunc-
tion and tricuspid regurgitation with pul-
monary vasodilators (milrinone and NO) 
and inotropes will be necessary for patients 
who manifest severe right ventricular dys-
function after LVAD implantation. Severe 
right ventricular dysfunction will produce 
a low LVAD output in conjunction with a 
high CVP and tricuspid regurgitation. 
Right ventricular distension and hypokine-
sis seen with TEE are valuable in guiding 
therapy to reduce tricuspid regurgitation 
and improve right ventricular function. In 
some circumstances, a tricuspid annulo-
plasty may be warranted at the time of 
LVAD implantation. If all these maneuvers 
fail to support the right heart, the patient 
should be converted to biventricular assist 
or ECMO.
The following causes should be considered 
in decreased preload conditions.
●
●Hypovolemia.
●
●Poor positioning/obstruction of the inflow 
cannula.
●
●Impaired right ventricular function with 
delivery of inadequate volumes of blood 
across the pulmonary circulation to an 
LVAD.

It is important to realize that in patients 
with nonpulsatile continuous-­flow devices, 
the arterial waveform will a nonpulsatile or 
minimally pulsatile representation of the 
mean arterial blood pressure (MAP). Given 
the inverse relationship between delta P 
and LVAD flow, it is generally desirable to 
keep MAP <80–90 mmHg. A detailed sum-
mary of the management of hemodynamic 
instability in patients following implanta-
tion of a pulsatile VAD is presented in 
Figure 10.9 while management of a contin-
uous axial or centrifugal pump VAD is pre-
sented in Figure 10.10.
BiVAD Insertion
During BiVAD placement, the possibility of 
pulmonary endothelial injury, pulmonary 
edema, and hemorrhage exists when high 
flows are abruptly directed into the pulmo-
nary vascular bed. Patients with elevated pul-
monary arterial pressure due to inadequate 
left atrial decompression or elevated PVR are 
particularly at risk for this problem.

Structured Hand-­off 
from OR to CICU Team
Postoperative care commences with a 
­structured hand-­off of the patient from the 
OR team to the CICU team. The precise 
­process varies from institution to institution, 
but the format is generally conducted as 
illustrated in Figures 11.1 and 11.2.
The final summary by the CICU team 
should include an assessment of hemody-
namic goals, postoperative procedures to be 
performed (such as tube/line removal and 
chest closure), cardiopulmonary status, physi-
ologic vulnerabilities (particularly residual 
lesions), and the intended duration of mechan-
ical ventilation. Based on this assessment, the 
projected trajectory for each patient can be 
determined. Intelligent choices regarding use 
of sedatives, analgesics, and, if necessary, neu-
romuscular blocking agents (NMBA) can then 
be made. Since no one drug can provide anal-
gesia, sedation, and muscle relaxation, the use 
of multiple agents is necessary.
Once the hand-­off is complete, the CICU 
must carefully define the patient’s anticipated 
postoperative trajectory and then coordinate 
sedation strategies, inotrope and vasodilator 
therapy, nutrition, hemostasis management, 
and ventilation strategy. For most patients, 
the postoperative recovery is uncomplicated. 
However, when the patient’s clinical progress 
or postoperative cardiorespiratory function 
does not follow the expected course, myocar-
dial function must be assessed, and the 
­presence and significance of residual defects 
must be determined with echocardiography, 
­cardiac catheterization, or both.
Sedation/Analgesia 
Medications
Sedation/analgesia, alone or in combination 
with NMBAs, is generally required for chil-
dren in the CICU receiving mechanical 
­ventilation and can be achieved with combi-
nations of benzodiazepines, hypnotic agents 
such as ketamine and propofol, and the 
alpha-­2-­agonist dexmedetomidine.
An important consideration with the use 
of a continuous infusion of a medication in 
the CICU is the concept of context-­sensitive 
half-­time, which is the time required for 
blood or plasma concentrations of a drug to 
decrease by 50% after discontinuation of 
drug administration. During an infusion, 
IV drugs with multicompartmental pharma-
cokinetics initially distribute in the ­central 
compartment with subsequent redistribu-
tion to peripheral compartments. When 
these peripheral redistribution sites become 
saturated and the concentration of drug in 
them reaches equilibrium with the central 
compartment, the context-­sensitive half-­
time becomes equal to the terminal elimina-
tion half-­life. A practical example is fentanyl, 
which is highly lipophilic and initially has a 
short half-­life due to redistribution from the 
central compartment to adipose tissue. Once 
adipose tissue becomes saturated, fentanyl 
loses its short-­duration characteristics such

that after a three-­hour infusion the short-­
acting opioid fentanyl has a longer half-­time 
than a morphine infusion once the infusions 
are stopped. The context-­sensitive half-­
times of analgesic and sedative medications 
commonly used in the CICU are illustrated 
in Figure 11.3.
Benzodiazepines
Benzodiazepines are commonly used as 
sedative-­hypnotic agents for children in the 
CICU; these agents have no intrinsic analge-
sic activity. Midazolam is the most com-
monly used benzodiazepine, with a rapid 
onset and short duration of action, and a 
short context-­sensitive half-­life. It is gener-
ally administered via IV using either inter-
mittent bolus doses (0.025–0.1 mg kg–1) or as 
a continuous infusion 0.05–0.2 mg kg–1 h–1 
when early extubation is not anticipated. 
Prolonged infusions are associated with 
development of tolerance and subsequent 
physical dependence, leading to withdrawal 
symptoms and delirium.
Opioids
Opioids are the mainstay of pain manage-
ment in the CICU. In addition, they possess 
some sedative activity and are used to 
blunt  sympathetic responses to noxious 
­stimulation such as endotracheal tube 
­suctioning. Morphine is the prototypical opi-
ate and ­provides excellent analgesia when 
­administered either as ­intermittent bolus 
doses (0.05–0.2 mg kg–1) or as a continuous 
infusion (0.01–0.03 mg kg–1 h–1) when early 
extubation is not anticipated. It is important 
to remember that a typical bolus dose of mor-
phine achieves a peak effect in 10–20 minutes 
and has a duration of action of approximately 
2–4 hours. Morphine has little effect on blood 
pressure and heart rate in normovolemic 
patients. However, high doses in critically 
ill  patients can lead to decreased systemic 
­vascular resistance (SVR), increased venous 
capacitance, and inhibition of baroreceptor 
reflexes, causing  hypotension. In addition, 
morphine ­stimulates the release of histamine, 
which contributes to the development of 
hypotension.
Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that is 
70–100 times more potent than morphine. It 
has minimal effects on hemodynamics and is 
commonly administered to critically ill, 
hemodynamically unstable children both as a 
bolus doses (1–2 μg kg–1) and as a continuous 
infusion (1-­3 μg kg–1 min–1). Tolerance to fen-
tanyl develops more rapidly and the risk of 
dependence and withdrawal phenomena is 
greater than with morphine.
Sufentanil is 5–10 times more potent 
than fentanyl and 1000 times more potent 
than morphine. It has excellent context-­
sensitive half-­time kinetics but is rarely 
used as a ­continuous infusion in the CICU 
due to extremely rapid development of tol-
erance. Remifentanil is a very short-­acting,

pure μ-­receptor agonist that is equipotent 
to fentanyl. Its rapid onset and offset times 
and lack of significant hemodynamic effects 
make it particularly useful as a continuous 
infusion (0.4–1 μg kg–1 min–1) for proce-
dural analgesia and anesthesia, and less 
useful for prolonged sedation in the CICU, 
and its context-­sensitive half-­time remains 
constant at four minutes regardless of infu-
sion duration.
Propofol
Propofol is an IV-­administered sedative-­
hypnotic agent. It has no intrinsic analgesic 
properties. Propofol has a fast onset time 
with an effect seen within 40 seconds of injec-
tion. It has a large volume of distribution and 
an increased clearance in children when com-
pared with adults. It takes 1–3  minutes for 
blood–brain equilibration to occur and there-
fore dose adjustments are not recommended 
sooner than 3–5 minutes, allowing time for a 
clinical effect. The context-­sensitive half-­time 
for an infusion duration of up to eight hours is 
less than 40  minutes, allowing rapid emer-
gence from its effects. Unfortunately, the very 
narrow therapeutic index of this drug leaves 
little margin for error with sedation, rapidly 
progressing to unconsciousness and apnea. 
Despite this and other risks that accompany 
the use of propofol in critically ill cardiac 
patients, including bradycardia, decreased 
SVR, hypotension, and reduced clearance, it 
is commonly used in early tracheal extuba-
tion protocols.
The current package insert for propofol 
contains the following language: “Propofol 
injectable emulsion is not indicated for use in 
PICU sedation since the safety of this regi-
men has not been established.” Nonetheless, 
propofol is used at low doses (<4 mg kg–1 h–1 
or 67 μg kg–1 min–1) alone or in combination 
with other drugs, generally in older patients, 
to provide short sedation. Enthusiasm for the 
use of propofol in critically ill children must 
be tempered by the concern for the develop-
ment of the propofol infusion syndrome, the 
risk factors for which appear to be an ­infusion 
rate of 4 mg kg–1 h–1 or 67 μg kg–1 min–1 for 
longer than 48 hours, young age, critical ill-
ness, concomitant catecholamine infusions, 
and concomitant steroid supplementation. 
Many institutions do not encourage or allow 
propofol infusions for sedation of children 
for more than 24–48 hours.
Dexmedetomidine
Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective central 
nervous system alpha-­2-­adrenergic receptor 
agonist with a large volume of distribution 
(necessitating a loading dose), an initial short 
half-­life allowing titration during continuous 
infusion, and a prolonged context-­sensitive 
half-­time (four hours after an eight-­hour infu-
sion). It produces sedation and benzodiazepine-­
sparing effects as well as weak analgesia/
opioid-­sparing effects by increasing GABA 
inhibition in the central nervous system and 
spinal cord. The central nervous system effects 
of therapeutic plasma levels of dexmedetomi-
dine resemble those of nonrapid eye move-
ment stage 2 (light) sleep. Dexmedetomidine 
has minimal effect on respiratory function.
Therapeutic plasma levels of dexmedetomi-
dine obtained during continuous infusion 
(0.5–1.5 μg kg–1 h–1) allow lower amounts of 
opioid and benzodiazepine infusions to be uti-
lized. As such, dexmedetomidine may help 
avoid the development of opioid and benzo-
diazepine dependence, ameliorate withdrawal 
symptoms, and prevent postoperative delir-
ium. Sedation in children with dexmedeto-
midine alone is not practical in the intensive 
care setting given that large doses of 
­dexmedetomidine (2–3 μg kg–1 h–1), with 
their associated hemodynamic effects, are 
necessary. Withdrawal following prolonged 
dexmedetomidine infusions is problem-
atic,  with the most common manifestations 
being transient hypertension, agitation, and 
­tachyarrhythmias. Slow weaning with transi-
tion to a nonparenteral alpha-­2-­adrenergic 
receptor agonist such as a clonidine transder-
mal patch is usually necessary.
There is some evidence that the prevalence 
of perioperative junctional ectopic ­tachycardia 
Postoperative Cardiac Intensive Care Unit Care
131
and supraventricular tachycardia is lower in 
patients receiving dexmedetomidine and that 
dexmedetomidine administration may be use-
ful in terminating arrhythmias.
Ketamine
Ketamine is structurally related to phencycli-
dine and blocks the N-­methyl-­D-­aspartate 
receptor. It acts on the cortex and limbic sys-
tem, leading to a dissociative anesthetic state 
with strong analgesic, sedative, and antegrade 
amnestic effects during which there is mainte-
nance of the airway reflexes. While multiple 
routes of administration are available, IV and 
intramuscular administrations are preferred 
for procedural sedation and analgesia. 
Ketamine has a short context-­sensitive half-­
time (40  min after discontinuation of an 
egight-­hour infusion), making it an ideal agent 
for a continuous infusion. Ketamine infusions 
(0.5–1.5  mg kg–1 h–1) can be utilized in the 
CICU to provide analgesia, sedative, and a dis-
sociative state, as well as to provide opioid and 
benzodiazepines “holidays” in patients requir-
ing long-­term sedation.
Management of Sedation/
Analgesia
Management of sedation, analgesia, and 
NMB agents, and prevention of the develop-
ment of delirium and iatrogenic withdrawal 
syndrome (IWS) are major challenges in crit-
ically ill pediatric patients, particularly those 
who require prolonged CICU stays. In 
patients six years old and older who can 
­communicate, pain assessment via self-­
report can be performed using the Visual 
Analog Scale, the Numeric Rating Scale, the 
Oucher Scale, or the Wong-­Baker Faces pain 
scale. The Faces, Legs, Activity, Cry, and 
Consolability (FLACC) or COMFORT-­B 
scales can be used in assessing pain in 
­noncommunicative pediatric patients. The 
COMFORT-­B Scale or the State Behavioral 
Scale (Figure 11.4) can be used to assess the 
level of sedation in mechanically ventilated 
pediatric patients. The Cornell Assessment 
of Pediatric Delirium (CAPD) for children 
0–18 years and the Pediatric Confusion 
Assessment Method for the ICU (pCAM-­
ICU) for children older than five years are 
the most widely used assessment tools for 
delirium. The Sophia Observation Scale and 
the Withdrawal Assessment Tool-­1 are both 
pediatric 
withdrawal 
symptom 
grading 
scales. An example of a coordinated approach 
utilizing these various scales and the com-
plex interplay between the various compo-
nents is illustrated in Figure 11.5.
Detection and Treatment 
of Low Cardiac Output 
Syndrome
Low cardiac output syndrome (LCOS) is 
defined as clinical signs or symptoms (tachy-
cardia, oliguria, poor perfusion, or cardiac 
arrest) with or without a widened arterial-­
mixed venous oxygen saturation difference or 
metabolic ­acidosis, and with or without ele-
vated blood lactate or rapid increase in blood 
lactate. Strictly defined LCOS is a cardiac index 
(CI) ≤2 l min–2 m2. Once LCOS is identified, 
the ­following factors must be considered.
●
●Residual anatomic defects such as a large 
VSD or severe RV or LV outflow tract 
obstruction.
●
●Postcardiotomy dysfunction such as RV dys-
function following a right ventriculotomy.
●
●Compromised coronary artery from ana-
tomic causes.
●
●Supraventricular or ventricular dysrhyth-
mias or loss of atrioventricular conduction.
●
●Low preload due to ongoing bleeding.
●
●Systemic vasoconstriction and high SVR.
●
●Metabolic derangements such as hypocal-
cemia and hypomagnesemia.
●
●Pulmonary hypertension.
●
●Low hematocrit and compromise of 
­systemic oxygen delivery (Chapter 7).
Nevertheless, a cardiac output decline of 
approximately 30% should be anticipated 
The Pediatric Cardiac Anesthesia Handbook
132
within 9–12 hours after surgery, even if the 
surgical repair is adequate. Vasoactive infu-
sions are often needed to mitigate the 
decreased cardiac output in these patients. 
Dopamine and epinephrine are commonly 
used for inotropy, while milrinone may be 
added to reduce ventricular afterload. Ideally, 
afterload reduction, or the reduction in sys-
tolic intraventricular wall tension, is initiated 
to improve ventriculoarterial coupling. That 
is, afterload reduction strategies are intended 
to achieve better matching of ventricular 
contractility to the impedance characteris-
tics of the arterial circulation such that stroke 
volume (SV), CI and systemic oxygen deliv-
ery (DO2) can be optimized. Ideally, myocar-
dial O2 demands should be minimized, while 
preload, heart rate and rhythm, and myocar-
dial contractility (if possible) should be 
­optimized to derive the most benefit from a 
hemodynamic support strategy emphasizing 
systemic afterload reduction.
To better understand the use of inodilator 
therapy, a thorough grasp of ventriculoarterial 
coupling is required. The most illustrative way 
to approach this analysis is with the use of ven-
tricular pressure–volume loops (Figure 11.6). 
The slope of the straight line generated by con-
necting the ventricular end-­systolic pressure–
volume points defines time-­varying ventricular 
elastance, which represents the contractile 
state and stiffness of the ventricle. Effective 
arterial elastance (Ea) derived from ventricular 
pressure–­volume loops is a measure of after-
load. Ea lumps the nonpulsatile and pulsatile 
­components of arterial load into a single num-
ber but does not provide information on their 
relative contributions.

The effects of vasodilator therapy on SV and 
blood pressure in a particular patient will be 
dependent on the existing ventriculoarterial 
coupling. This concept is illustrated in 
Figure 11.7 by observing the effects of utilizing 
milrinone or sodium nitroprusside as a vasodi-
lator in two patients with very different ven-
triculoarterial coupling characteristics: one 
with depressed ventricular contractility, such 
as a heart failure patient or a patient with post-
cardiotomy LCOS, and the other with hyper-
dynamic ventricular function, such as a patient 
with left ventricular concentric hypertrophy 
following relief of LVOT obstruction (coarcta-
tion repair, subaortic membrane resection, 
aortic valve surgery for AS). Sodium nitro-
prusside reduces afterload by reducing periph-
eral resistance and ­increasing large vessel 
compliance, which reduces pulse-­wave veloc-
ity and wave reflection. When ventricular 
function is reduced, ­vasodilator therapy that 
reduces Ea results in substantial improve-
ments in SV and cardiac output with little or 
no change in blood pressure and a substantial 
reduction in left atrial pressure. This left atrial 
pressure reduction then produces a significant 
reduction in pulmonary artery pressure 
regardless of the pulmonary vascular resist-
ance. When the left ventricle is hyperdynamic 
and stiff, as occurs in concentric hypertrophy, 
vasodilator therapy that reduces Ea results in 
profound hypotension with no substantial 
improvement in SV or cardiac output. Such 
hypotension is exacerbated in cases of hypo-
volemia (such as bleeding postoperative 
patients) and is ­especially disadvantageous to 
these patients because it compromises suben-
docardial ­perfusion, particularly in cases of 
reflex tachycardia.
There are numerous approaches to treat-
ment of LCOS but regardless of the initial 
choice of agents, there must be a consist-
ent reassessment of CI and DO2. For exam-
ple,  combining low-­dose epinephrine or 
­dopamine with an IV afterload-­reducing 
agent such as milrinone is frequently benefi-
cial to support patients with significant ven-
tricular dysfunction accompanied by elevated

each loop. The slope for fixed afterload is the same for each loop. This can be seen in loop 2 and loop 4. Despite

Mechanical Ventilation
The requirement for postoperative mechani-
cal ventilation is determined by the extent of 
altered lung mechanics, ventilation/perfusion 
abnormalities and intrapulmonary shunt pre-
sent. When initiated, the effects of positive-­
pressure ventilation (PPV) on intrathoracic 
pressure and subsequently on cardiac func-
tion and ventricular interaction must be 
considered. These changes as compared to 
spontaneous ventilation are summarized in 
Figure 11.8 and are as follows.
●
●PPV increases pleural pressure and pro-
duces changes opposite to those seen dur-
ing spontaneous breathing.
●
●During the inspiratory phase of PPV, RV 
preload is reduced and RV afterload is 
increased.
●
●During the inspiratory phase of PPV, LV 
preload increases as positive pressure 
enhances blood flow from the pulmonary 
veins.
●
●During the inspiratory phase of PPV, LV 
afterload is reduced due to a decrease in 
the transmural pressure of the LV relative 
to the extrathoracic aorta.
As a result, LV stroke volume and MAP 
increase at the end of the inspiratory phase of 
PPV. At the end of the expiratory period, 
both LV stroke volume and MAP decrease 
consequent to a reduction in LV preload. 
This delayed reduction in LV preload is due 
to the 2–3-­second transpulmonary blood 
transit time for the decreased venous return 
and RV preload during late inspiration/early 
expiration to manifest as a reduction of LV 
preload during end-­expiration.
Patients with normal RV compliance and 
without residual volume load or pressure 
load on the ventricle after surgery usually 
show little change in RV function from the 
alteration in preload and afterload with PPV. 
However, these effects can be magnified in 
patients with restrictive RV physiology after 
congenital heart surgery. Neonates with dias-
tolic dysfunction following a right ventricul-
otomy such as necessary to repair TOF, 
pulmonary atresia, or truncus arteriosus, or 
those with concentric RV hypertrophy due to 
RVOT obstruction are especially sensitive to 
increased RV afterload from PPV. In this set-
ting, an increase in RV afterload can lead to 
RV distention, septal shift, and reduced LV 
compliance and filling.
The effects of PPV on LV function are most 
evident in patients with LV dysfunction with 
elevated preload and afterload. Here, the 
reduction in preload and afterload can result 
in an increase in the cardiac output and a 
reduction in myocardial oxygen demand. In 
addition, patients with LV dysfunction may 
have impaired pulmonary mechanics second-
ary to increased lung water, decreased lung 
compliance, and increased airway resistance. 
Neonates and infants fatigue early because of 
limited respiratory reserve. Furthermore, a 
significant proportion of total body oxygen 
consumption is directed at the increased 
work of breathing in neonates and infants 
with LV dysfunction, contributing to poor 
feeding and failure to thrive. PPV has an addi-
tional benefit in these patients by reducing 
the work of breathing and oxygen demand. In 
general, with their limited physiologic reserve, 
neonates and infants should not be weaned 
from mechanical ventilation until hemody-
namic stability is accompanied by resolution 
of intrapulmonary shunt and altered respira-
tory mechanics.
Most patients wean from PPV without diffi-
culty but some patients with borderline cardiac 
function and a significant residual lesion 
­burden may require prolonged mechanical 
ventilation and a slower weaning process. Most
